name: Word Form
summary: Choosing the right noun, verb, adjective or adverb form.

sections.title: Word Form: Choosing the Right Part of Speech
sections.label: Introduction

paragraphs: Many English words belong to a family: economy, economic, economical, economically. Each member has the same basic meaning but a different job in the sentence. Nouns name things, verbs show actions, adjectives describe nouns, and adverbs describe verbs or adjectives.

A word form error happens when you choose the right family but the wrong member, for example an economy problem instead of an economic problem. Your reader usually understands you, but the sentence sounds clearly wrong. Learning to check the job of each word is the key to avoiding these errors.

blocks.title: The rule in one line
blocks.text: Right word, right job: a noun for things, a verb for actions, an adjective before a noun, an adverb for a verb.

paragraphs: Word form errors count against both Lexical Resource and Grammatical Range and Accuracy, so they can affect two of your four writing scores. Because IELTS rewards a range of vocabulary, learners often try new words, and that is exactly when word form slips appear.
The most frequent problems are adjective vs. adverb in Task 1 (a significant increase vs. increased significantly) and noun vs. adjective in Task 2 (poverty vs. poor).

Before the rules, look at how a word family works. One idea can appear in up to four forms, and each form fits a different position in the sentence. Learning words in families, not one by one, is the best long-term fix.

sections.title: Rule 1: Use word endings as clues
sections.label: Rule 1: Use word endings as clues

paragraphs: Word endings (suffixes) often tell you what part of speech a word is. They are not a perfect guide, but they help you notice when a form looks wrong in a particular position.
For example, if a word ends in -tion, it is almost certainly a noun, so it cannot describe another noun or act as a verb.

rows: environmental, successful, effective, dangerous, affordable, economic

sections.title: Rule 2: Adjective before a noun, adverb after a verb
sections.label: Rule 2: Adjective before a noun, adverb after a verb

paragraphs: This is the rule that matters most for Task 1. If you are describing a noun (an increase, a fall), use an adjective: a significant increase. If you are describing a verb (increased, fell), use an adverb: increased significantly.
Both structures are useful, and mixing them gives your report variety. Just make sure the form matches the word it describes.

items.text: There was a sharply rise in prices.
There was a sharp rise in prices.

sections.title: Rule 3: Nouns for subjects and objects
sections.label: Rule 3: Nouns for subjects and objects

paragraphs: The subject and the object of a sentence must be nouns (or noun phrases). A common mistake is to use an adjective or a verb in these positions, for example Unemployed is rising when you mean Unemployment is rising.
Ask yourself: am I naming a thing or an idea here? If so, you need the noun form.

items.text: Unemployed is rising in many countries.
Unemployment is rising in many countries.
Education is the key to success and happy.
Education is the key to success and happiness.
The develop of technology has changed our lives.
The development of technology has changed our lives.

sections.title: Rule 4: Adjectives after be, become and seem
sections.label: Rule 4: Adjectives after be, become and seem

paragraphs: After linking verbs such as be, become, seem, look and feel, use an adjective. These verbs describe a state, not an action, so the word after them describes the subject.
Compare: She looks happy (adjective, describing her) and She looked happily at the results (adverb, describing how she looked).
Some word pairs look very similar but have different meanings. Mixing them up is a common error that examiners notice quickly.
The pairs below are the ones most likely to appear in IELTS essays.

rows: related to the economy / saving money
important in history / about the past
a positive effect; pollution affects health

sections.title: Rule 6: -ed or -ing? And words for people
sections.label: Rule 6: -ed or -ing? And words for people

paragraphs: Adjectives ending in -ed describe how a person feels (interested, bored, worried). Adjectives ending in -ing describe the thing that causes the feeling (interesting, boring, worrying).
Similarly, many word families have a separate noun for a person: economy → economist, science → scientist, employ → employee or employer.

items.text: Many students feel boring in long lectures.
Many students feel bored in long lectures.

sections.title: Rule 7: Base verbs after modals and to
sections.label: Rule 7: Base verbs after modals and to

paragraphs: After modal verbs (can, should, must, will) and after to, use the base form of the verb, not a noun or an adjective. Governments should invest is correct; Governments should investment is not.
This error often appears when a learner knows the noun better than the verb, so it is worth learning both forms together.

items.text: The aim is to reduction pollution.
The aim is to reduce pollution.

paragraphs: To make an adjective stronger or weaker, put an adverb in front of it: extremely important, relatively small, highly effective. Using an adjective instead (extreme important) is a common slip.
This structure is useful in both tasks, especially with words like significantly, relatively, increasingly and highly.

items.text: This is an extreme important issue.
This is an extremely important issue.

paragraphs: Here is how correct word forms look in real IELTS writing.

rows: There was a sharp rise in 2015.
Poverty is a major cause of crime.

paragraphs: These five errors are among the most common word form mistakes in IELTS essays.
Use this routine on the key words of each sentence.

steps: For each important word, ask what job it does: naming (noun), action (verb), describing a noun (adjective), describing a verb or adjective (adverb).
Check the form matches the job, especially after a / the, after be and after Task 1 verbs.
Watch the confusing pairs: economic / economical, effect / affect.

furtherStudy.title: George Mason University: Choosing the Correct Word Form
furtherStudy.description: How to choose between noun, verb, adjective and adverb forms.

cards.front: There was a ____ increase in sales.
cards.why: Increase is a noun, so it is described by an adjective.

cards.front: The price of oil rose ____ in 2022.
cards.why: Rose is a verb, so it is described by an adverb.

cards.front: ____ is a serious problem in many cities.
cards.why: The subject of a sentence must be a noun. Unemployed is an adjective.

cards.front: Regular exercise is ____ for your health.
cards.why: After is, we need an adjective to describe the subject.

cards.front: The government should ____ more in education.
cards.why: After should, we need the base form of the verb.
The lectures cause the feeling, so we use the -ing adjective.

cards.front: The country has enjoyed strong ____ growth.
cards.why: Economic means related to the economy. Economical means saving money.

cards.front: Online learning is ____ popular among adults.
cards.why: An adverb is needed before the adjective popular.
After can, we need a verb. Affect is the verb; effect is usually a noun.

cards.front: The ____ of technology has changed our lives.
cards.why: After the, we need a noun.
